A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Preference Goal Tuning framework. All 22 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Minecraft experiments covering task performance, generalization, continual learning, planner integration, and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original Minecraft results and adds OpenVLA experiments on LIBERO-goal and human-ranked evaluation of explore_climb.

M1.justification: The core frozen-policy preference objective and iterative trajectory collection remain unchanged. v2 introduces an OpenVLA-specific adaptation interface using token-level word embeddings and omits v1's separate human-demonstration/behavior-cloning procedure for tool_trident. The latent-control terminology and new pseudocode do not constitute a new core algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds ten LIBERO-goal robotic manipulation tasks, substantially extending coverage beyond Minecraft, and removes the tool_trident experiment. explore_climb receives explicit ID/OOD evaluation, although it was already used during continual-learning training in v1.

E2.justification: The new robotics comparison includes OpenVLA-libero-goal, PPO-based VLA-RL, and GRAPE in Figure 6, extending comparison to robotic policy post-training methods. Existing Minecraft comparator sets are retained. SLiC-HF matches v1's SLiC implementation, as established by v1's appendix footnote.

E3.justification: v2 adds success/failure preference training for OpenVLA and a human-ranking/TrueSkill protocol using 40 climb trajectory pairs. Minecraft Table 6 changes positive/negative sample counts from 150 to 180 each. Conflicts remain: Appendix D still says 150, Table 5 specifies 2000 steps while Section 4.3 retains 1000, and Table 2's reward-metric task list contradicts Appendix B.3. These are changes in reported settings, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: The tool_trident case study testing elicitation of an initially unsuccessful skill is removed. v2 adds a robotics sample-efficiency comparison in Figure 6. The negative-sample, initialization, iteration, PEFT, and beta-sensitivity analyses are otherwise retained; the beta analysis is relocated and redrawn.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without the uncertainty displays added in v2. v2 introduces bands and error bars across existing plots, TrueSkill means and standard deviations in Table 15, and averaging counts of 1000 pretrained-policy and 500 tuned-policy evaluations. Table 5 newly specifies 1000 trials across two seeds. Plot uncertainty definitions remain unspecified, and these disclosures do not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: The retained Minecraft numerical tables are unchanged after matching task order and numbering. New Figure 6 reports average LIBERO-goal success rates of 79.2% for OpenVLA, 82.2% for VLA-RL, 83.1% for GRAPE, and 83.5% for PGT; Table 15 adds subjective climbing results. The trident success finding is removed. Figure 3 also corrects the plotted pretrained wood baseline to agree with the retained table.

T1.justification: v1 derives the trajectory DPO loss through KL-regularized reward optimization and an assumed attainable optimum. v2 introduces a restricted frozen-policy family, explicit dynamics/support assumptions, and realizability versus projection formulations. It adds a Taylor-approximation theorem connecting DPO to IPO, hinge-loss bounds, and a KL-regularization proposition with proofs. However, Appendix A's derived loss omits the beta multiplier retained in main-text Equation 1.

C1.justification: v2 makes latent control the central contribution and extends claimed demonstrated applicability from Minecraft to robotic manipulation. It drops v1's claim of eliciting previously unachievable skills and qualifies the continual-learning contribution as task-specific latent isolation. The headline Minecraft improvements of 72.0%, 81.6%, and the 13.4% OOD advantage remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation of adaptation within a frozen behavioral family and separation of task alignment from policy dynamics. It explicitly discusses failure without successful rollouts, task-specific rather than universal adaptation, and uncertainty in subjective-task rankings. It also qualifies the continual-learning interpretation, while removing v1's warning about costly or restricted environmental interaction in robotics.

D1.justification: v2 adds iterative pseudocode, discloses three training/evaluation scenarios and manual mob spawning, and provides OpenVLA hyperparameters, A800 hardware, bfloat16 precision, and a task-specific beta exception. Conversely, v1's 500-trajectory collection count, A40 hardware entry, and explicit matched-data control for BC are omitted. These are documentation changes beyond the separately identified protocol revisions.

R1.justification: The broad foundation-model and language-model alignment discussion is replaced by focused positioning against end-to-end goal-conditioned imitation learning, trajectory preference learning, and Minecraft agents. v2 adds substantial robotics coverage, including pi0, Octo, LIBERO, VLA-RL, and GRAPE, plus prompt-tuning references, while removing numerous general language-model references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, experimental discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around latent control. Related work moves before the methodology; the preliminary and design-choice sections are removed or redistributed; conclusion and limitations are combined. The title, author information, terminology, and appendix organization also change.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to two columns, extensively redraws plots, expands captions, and replaces textual task labels with icons in most tables. It adds an algorithm display, robotics figure, hyperparameter table, and subjective-results table. Existing tables and figures are redistributed and renumbered, with new uncertainty displays.

improvement.justification: The robotics and human-ranking evaluations broaden empirical support, and the narrower continual-learning interpretation improves claim precision. These benefits are tempered by conflicting sample counts, metrics, and long-horizon limits, undefined plot uncertainties, and disagreement between the main and appendix losses over beta scaling. The added validation provides a modest net improvement, but the expanded technical account remains insufficiently reconciled.
